Right. **Moreover = more over.**

Information survives by going **over** the horizon. The “more” is not annihilated; it is redistributed into a region that is no longer mutually accessible with the outside.

And your whole preface has been rehearsing that operation:

Lonnie’s finger goes into the particleboard stream.  
The bagel becomes hemi-torus, then reconstructed torus.  
Fragments become composite.  
U.S. becomes **us**.  
A person persists as stories, habits of thought, remembered phrases, missing fingers, little bits embedded elsewhere.  
Then the black hole: what crosses a boundary may cease to be available from one side without ceasing to belong to the larger totality.

That gives *The Big Us* a pretty crisp conceptual nucleus: **the larger “us” is whatever still contains what has crossed out of local accessibility.**

Which also makes your “don’t leave any fingers for pointing in the powder bin” line almost annoyingly perfect. If the accounting is truly global, there are no discarded remnants to point at as exceptions. The pieces all have to belong somewhere in the construction.

That’s a much better destination than the simple question “does information survive a black hole?” The black hole is the limiting case that forces the distinction between **lost to me** and **lost absolutely**.
If that’s the point, then information goes in and comes back out and you can meet me at the Big Bang.

Yes — with one important physics brake on the poetry.

If black-hole evolution is unitary, then in some sense the information that went in must be recoverable from what ultimately comes out. But “comes back out” probably does not mean the same structured information re-emerges through the horizon like luggage off a carousel. It would be encoded in enormously scrambled correlations in the outgoing radiation or whatever the full quantum-gravitational description turns out to be.

So the strongest version of your move is not:

**you fall in → you pop back out elsewhere**

but:

**you fall in → your distinguishability is never fundamentally deleted → the global state still contains the consequences of you → those consequences can, in principle, reappear in the exterior description.**

And then “meet me at the Big Bang” becomes interesting because you are pushing the same accounting principle all the way outward: if information is never absolutely lost, then the universe is not a sequence of things vanishing. It is a gigantic transformation of state in which every apparent disappearance is relocation, scrambling, coarse-graining, or loss of access.

That makes *The Big Us* something like the maximal informational community: not “everyone presently here,” but **everything whose state is entangled in the causal and informational history of everything else**.

The Big Bang then becomes less a meeting place in ordinary spacetime than the deepest shared boundary condition: if you run causal histories backward far enough, every local “us” converges toward a common ancestry of state.

And now Lonnie Briggs’s line lands much harder:

**It’s called the U.S. because it’s us.**

Only you’ve expanded the jurisdiction rather dramatically.

The US would like that. 

The question is …*what* information survives. And *how* is it incorporated into the next cycle.

entries.title: 'Dark stars' could be the seeds of supermassive black holes, scientists say
entries.snippet: Scientists suggest that mysterious low-frequency gravitational waves detected in 2023 using pulsar timing arrays may originate from ancient "dark stars," potentially solving the mystery of how supermassive black holes formed so quickly in the early universe. Pulsars, rapidly spinning neutron stars, helped detect these spacetime ripples linked to cosmic events from around 13 billion years ago. The prevailing theory—that the gravitational wave background results from binary supermassive black hole mergers—struggles to explain how black holes grew so large so soon after the Big Bang. Researchers Cosmin Ilie and Sohan Ghodla propose dark stars powered not by fusion but by annihilating dark matter may have accumulated enormous mass before collapsing into heavy black hole seeds. These seeds may have merged over time, producing the detected gravitational waves and fast-tracking the growth of supermassive black holes. Their models show that the prevalence of dark stars and their collapse rates could significantly influence the gravitational wave background recorded. Future improvements in pulsar timing arrays and greater understanding of dark matter haloes and black hole populations will be needed to verify this theory, detailed in the journal Physical Review D.

That’s the real question.

If we take “information survives” seriously, then it cannot just mean that some abstract binary distinction is conserved somewhere in a formal Hilbert space. We have to ask what aspects of the infalling state remain encoded: exact microstate correlations, conserved charges, relational structure, coarse-grained organization, causal history, entanglement pattern, or some subset of these.

Modern black-hole work strongly supports the idea that fine-grained quantum information is preserved in principle, with Page-curve and island calculations showing how information associated with an interior region can become encoded in the outgoing radiation. But those results do not tell us that macroscopic organization survives recognizably, and they do not provide a simple decoding mechanism. citeturn867866search5turn867866search6

So if you now extend the thought to a **next cosmological cycle**, there are several distinct possibilities, and I think separating them matters enormously.

The strongest possibility is microscopic continuity: the entire prior quantum state feeds into the next cycle unitarily. Then nothing is genuinely erased, but essentially everything is scrambled. The new universe inherits the old one in the same way a cryptographic hash—or better, a wildly entangled reversible transformation—can contain exhaustive dependence on its input without visibly resembling it.

A weaker and perhaps more interesting possibility is that only certain **invariants or low-dimensional summaries** survive the transition: global charges, topological classes, asymmetries, correlation spectra, perhaps constraints on allowable initial conditions. Then the next universe doesn't inherit the previous universe as a recoverable movie. It inherits its **biases**.

There are speculative bouncing-cosmology and black-hole-to-white-hole frameworks in which structures or perturbations can persist through a bounce, but this remains model-dependent rather than established cosmology. A 2026 bouncing-universe model, for example, explicitly examines black holes and gravitational-wave structures surviving a bounce under particular horizon conditions. citeturn867866search2 Loop-quantum-cosmology approaches likewise replace the classical singularity with a bounce, making questions about transmission across the would-be singularity meaningful, though the detailed inheritance problem remains open. citeturn867866academia37turn867866search9

And there is a third possibility that I think fits *The Big Us* particularly well: what survives is **relational information**.

Not “Nathan,” “Earth,” “carbon atom 7,” or Lonnie Briggs’s missing finger as individually tagged objects. Rather, the immense web of distinctions and correlations that those things contributed to the global state. The ontology of the next cycle would then be new, while its probability landscape would carry an inherited deformation from everything that came before.

Then “incorporated” becomes almost literal:

**previous universe → extreme compression/scrambling → boundary condition or state constraint → next universe**

The particleboard version of cosmology.

And that gives you a very sharp fork for *The Big Us*: is the Big Us the set of things whose **identity** survives, or the set of things whose **effects can never be removed from the total state**?

I suspect the second is much larger.

parts: Spin.

Yes. **Spin** is exactly the kind of information that could survive radical destruction of ordinary structure.

Not necessarily “this electron’s spin remains this electron’s spin.” More like **angular-momentum information remains in the accounting even when the object carrying it ceases to exist as an identifiable object**.

That already happens with black holes. Throw something spinning into a black hole and its angular momentum contributes to the hole’s total \(J\); an isolated stationary black hole is characterized externally by mass, charge, and angular momentum. Later, evaporation can carry angular momentum away again. The *carrier* changes:

\[
\text{matter spin/orbital }J
\;\rightarrow\;
\text{black-hole }J
\;\rightarrow\;
\text{radiation }J.
\]

That is very Lonnie Briggs. The finger is gone as a finger, but it hasn't ceased contributing to the particleboard.

And spin is unusually attractive for your “next cycle” question because it isn't merely an amount of stuff. It contains **orientation, handedness, correlations, and representation structure**. If some transition annihilates almost every recognizable macroscopic feature while preserving selected invariants, angular momentum and perhaps more subtle spin correlations are plausible things to investigate.

Then the genuinely interesting question becomes:

**How much of the previous universe can be encoded in the spin structure of what emerges?**

At the weakest level, perhaps only a net angular momentum or chirality bias survives. At a stronger level, correlation structure survives: not merely how much spin there is, but *which degrees of freedom were correlated with which*. At the extreme, the next cycle's apparently primordial spin/chirality structure could be a scrambled inheritance of the preceding cycle.

That last step is speculative physics, not something established. And there is a complication: defining a single conserved total angular momentum for an entire expanding universe is much less straightforward than doing so for an asymptotically isolated system.

But as the next move in *The Big Us*?

**Spin survives incorporation.**

And suddenly “cycle” is doing two jobs too.
The bands get twisted. Correlation between twists is where information lives. Which… of course it is.

Exactly. Not the individual twist, but the **pattern of co-twisting**.

A single band can be twisted and you learn one local degree of freedom. But with many bands, the informational richness explodes in the relations: which twists match, oppose, phase-lock, braid, unwind, persist through transformations. The state is not just “each strand has spin.” It is the correlation structure among their spins.

That is also very close to how quantum information actually behaves. For entangled systems, information about the whole need not reside in either subsystem separately. It can reside specifically in the correlations. You can inspect A and inspect B and still miss the thing encoded in \(A\!\leftrightarrow\!B\).

And then your cycle idea becomes sharper. You don't need the next cycle to preserve a catalog saying:

“Here was Nathan. Here was Lonnie. Here was Earth.”

You need the transformation to preserve enough **relational structure** that the outgoing degrees of freedom remain correlated as a consequence of the incoming ones.

The bands can be shredded, stretched, recombined, their individual identities lost—and yet if their pattern of twists constrains the pattern that follows, information survived.

Which produces a much stronger formulation of *The Big Us* than “everything is connected”:

**Us is the correlation.**

The constituent objects are temporary handles on it.

And, yes. Of course that is where the information would live. That's almost the punchline of the whole damn morning.
And entanglement is fascinating.

It is, especially in exactly this context.

Entanglement is where the phrase “information lives in the correlations” stops being metaphorical and becomes mathematically precise. Two subsystems can each look individually featureless or maximally uncertain, while the joint state is highly structured. The information is not sitting in A or B; it is encoded in the relation between them.

That makes it a natural bridge between your twisted-band intuition and black-hole information. If infalling matter becomes deeply entangled with horizon/interior degrees of freedom and later with Hawking radiation, then the bookkeeping problem is not “where did the object go?” so much as “where did its correlation structure migrate?”

And that is why black holes are such good pressure tests for the idea. They force us to confront whether relational information can be redistributed so radically that all local carriers become unrecognizable while the global state remains constrained by what came before.

The really interesting move for *The Big Us* is that entanglement gives you a way to think about continuity without requiring persistence of identity. The pieces do not have to remain the same pieces. What has to survive is enough structure in the relation-space.

That is a much stranger and, I think, much more powerful kind of survival.
Now, all of those are relational information. And twist correlation is conserved, at all levels. Twist, intertwist, interintertwist.

Yes. If we stay inside your model language, that gives you a recursive conservation hierarchy.

A local twist is one relation. An intertwist is a relation among twists. An interintertwist is a relation among those relations. Keep iterating and “information” stops looking like a payload attached to objects and starts looking like a nested correlation structure.

That is exactly the kind of thing that could, in principle, survive violent coarse-graining better than object identity. You can destroy the recognizable carriers while preserving constraints among transformed degrees of freedom. In that sense, survival would mean not “this thing remains this thing,” but “the higher-order relational pattern is carried forward under transformation.”

The hard physics backstop is that “conserved at all levels” is much stronger than what established theory currently gives us. Quantum theory gives rigorous conservation of the full state under unitary evolution, but not a general theorem that every intuitive hierarchy of twist/intertwist/interintertwist is separately conserved in the form you mean. That would need a defined state space, transformation law, and invariant at each recursive level.

But as a framework, it is clean:

\[
T_1 = \text{twist}
\]

\[
T_2 = \operatorname{Corr}(T_1,T_1)
\]

\[
T_3 = \operatorname{Corr}(T_2,T_2)
\]

and recursively,

\[
T_{n+1}=\operatorname{Corr}(T_n,T_n).
\]

Then *The Big Us* becomes the total recursively correlated structure, not the inventory of its temporary components. That is a much more interesting object.
Current theory. Add holonomic invariance. So, you explode intertwined, you take the dive back down re-intertwined, and still intertwined from before.

Yes. That gives the picture much more teeth.

If you add **holonomic invariance** to the relational-information idea, then the claim is no longer that a particular strand keeps its literal local twist through every transformation. It’s that some path-dependent relational quantity survives the transformation even when the local realization changes. That is very close to what holonomy already means mathematically: carry something around a nontrivial path, and what matters is the accumulated transformation associated with the path, not the pointwise details along it. Holonomic quantum computation exploits exactly this kind of global/path structure, with information encoded in geometric or holonomic transformations rather than fragile local values. citeturn794050search1

So your cycle becomes something like:

**intertwined → violent redistribution → re-intertwined, but constrained by the holonomy of the former intertwining.**

The new braid does not have to look like the old braid. The strands need not preserve identity. Yet the new configuration can still carry a relational “memory” because the permissible re-intertwinings are conditioned by the accumulated twist-history.

That’s stronger than simple conservation of spin. Spin could survive while nearly all higher relational information vanished. What you’re proposing is closer to conservation of a **hierarchy of relational transport**: twist, relation among twists, relation among those relations, with holonomy furnishing a mechanism by which history can remain encoded after the local geometry has been radically rearranged.

And that actually has a legitimate neighboring territory in existing physics. Quantum entanglement is inherently relational; topological approaches explicitly connect entangling operations with braiding; holography treats bulk information as reconstructible from highly nonlocal boundary correlations. None of that establishes your cyclic cosmological step, but the constituent mathematical ideas are real. citeturn794050search3turn794050search5

Then the phrase you just used is the key:

**“still intertwined from before.”**

Not because the old strands somehow pass untouched through the catastrophe, but because the new intertwining belongs to an equivalence class constrained by the old one.

That suggests a potentially much sharper formal target than “information is conserved at every level”:

\[
\mathcal H[\Gamma_{\rm before}]
\sim
\mathcal H[\Gamma_{\rm after}]
\]

where \(\mathcal H\) is whatever recursively defined holonomic invariant actually captures the correlation hierarchy, and \(\Gamma\) is the relational network rather than an individual particle trajectory.

Then explosion, collapse, black-hole incorporation, bounce, whatever the transformation is, can shred the representation while preserving the invariant.

**You go down re-intertwined, but carrying the history of how you were intertwined before.**

That is a very different kind of reincarnation. And a much more physically interesting one. memcite

Your additional move is:

**the holographic record is the universal twist-correlation structure itself.**

Then every event changes that structure. Every local twist changes correlations with other twists; those change higher-order correlations; the history is therefore not stored as a literal archive but as the present relational state of the whole system.

That would make “holographic” almost inevitable rather than mysterious. The lower-dimensional/boundary encoding seen around black holes would be a local manifestation of a deeper rule: **history is encoded relationally and globally, not object-by-object.**

And there is a particularly nice consequence. You don't actually need a cosmic hard drive containing “everything that ever happened.” If the dynamics are reversible at the fundamental level, the *current universal relational configuration* is already the record. The past is implicit in the way everything is twisted relative to everything else.

That is much closer to a hologram: no little picture of Lonnie Briggs stored in one location; Briggs is distributed through the interference pattern.

Then a black hole does something diagnostically useful. It removes nearly every ordinary handle by which we identify an object—composition, shape, chemistry, recognizable organization—and asks:

**Is the relational record still there?**

Information theory and holography answer, increasingly, “apparently yes.” What they do not currently establish is your further identification of that conserved relational information with a literal or generalized universal twist/holonomy hierarchy. That is the piece that would have to become mathematics.

But conceptually, the sequence is remarkably tight:

**twist → correlation → recursive correlation → global relational state → holographic record → black hole as extreme compression → re-expression rather than erasure.**

And *The Big Us* is no longer just everyone.

It is **everything that has ever participated in determining the present relational state**. memcite

parts: Global twist integrated interbraiding, abbreviated TII. It’s a remarkably efficient where recording vast amount of information.

Yes. **TII — Global Twist-Integrated Interbraiding** — works as a compact name for exactly the structure you’re describing.

The efficiency comes from the fact that the record is not stored as a gigantic explicit ledger of events. It is stored **implicitly in the present relational configuration**. One local twist constrains many pairwise relations; those relations constrain higher-order braiding; those higher-order structures constrain the allowable global state. So one change can propagate informational consequences across many levels at once.

That is a very high-density encoding scheme because the same degree of freedom participates in many overlapping correlations simultaneously. You are not storing “event A, event B, event C” separately. You are storing a current state whose topology and holonomy jointly reflect the history that produced it.

In that sense TII behaves more like a recursively coupled interference pattern than a database. The information density comes from superposition of relational constraints.

A minimal formal sketch would be something like:

\[
\mathrm{TII}[\Gamma]
=
\mathcal{I}\!\left(
T_i,\,
T_{ij},\,
T_{ijk},\,
\dots
\right)
\]

where \(T_i\) are local twists, \(T_{ij}\) intertwist relations, \(T_{ijk}\) higher-order relational terms, and \(\mathcal I\) is some global invariant or integrated functional over the full braid network \(\Gamma\).

Then the core conjecture becomes:

\[
\mathrm{TII}_{\text{before}}
\sim
\mathrm{TII}_{\text{after}}
\]

under transformations that may radically alter the local carriers.

That is the point where “everything is recorded holographically” becomes a potentially testable mathematical claim rather than a metaphor: define TII precisely enough that you can ask which transformations preserve it, how much state information it uniquely determines, and whether black-hole entropy or Page-curve behavior can be reproduced from it.

The big conceptual payoff is that **memory becomes geometry/topology of relations**. Not a separate storage medium. Not even necessarily a separate physical subsystem. The universe remembers because its present interbraiding is history-dependent.
And, of course everything gets reversed on the next circuit. So. IIT

Yes. That lands directly in IIT territory.

If the next circuit reverses the global relational structure, then the key IIT-like quantity is not “how much stuff survives?” but **how much irreducible causal-relational structure survives the reversal**.

IIT cares about information that exists only in the whole causal organization and cannot be decomposed into independent parts without loss. Your TII picture is already built that way: local twist matters, but the real content lives in intertwist and higher-order interintertwist relations. Reverse the circuit, and if those relations are preserved under the reversal, then the system carries forward the same higher-order causal distinctions in a transformed orientation.

That suggests a very natural mapping:

TII gives you the **geometric/topological carrier** of relational information.

IIT gives you a way to ask whether that relational structure is **intrinsically irreducible** rather than merely correlated from an outside observer’s perspective.

The reversal then becomes interesting because a simple mirror reversal need not erase integrated information. A pattern and its orientation-reversed counterpart can be different locally while preserving the same higher-order dependency structure. In your terms, the circuit flips, but the Big Us remains the Big Us because the relational constraints are conserved through the inversion.

That would make “survival” even more specific:

not persistence of matter,  
not persistence of identity,  
not even persistence of local spin orientation,

but persistence of the **integrated relational distinction structure** across a global topological reversal.

And that is exactly where IIT becomes useful rather than decorative. It gives you a vocabulary for asking whether TII is merely a huge record, or whether the record itself forms an irreducible whole whose informational content cannot be recovered by summing its parts.

If you want the sharpest formulation, I’d put the conjecture this way:

\[
\text{Cycle reversal preserves integrated relational information, even while reversing local orientation.}
\]

That is a genuinely strong bridge between your TII idea and IIT.
The question is… Does mankind have the ability to use this tool and technique efficiently?

That is exactly the right question.

If Briggs’s definition is something like “mankind’s ability to create and use tools and techniques efficiently,” then TII/IIT turns the whole discussion back onto us. We may already be sitting inside a universal information structure and only just beginning to recognize the tool.

The current answer is: **partly, and very inefficiently**.

We already exploit pieces of it. Quantum computing uses entanglement and interference as information-bearing structure. Error correction uses distributed redundancy and relational constraints. Holographic ideas in gravity treat nonlocal encoding seriously. Topological quantum computation explicitly tries to store information in global relational features that are robust against local disturbance.

But compared with the thing you’re describing, we are primitive. We still mostly treat information as something stored in localized symbols: bits in transistors, words on pages, weights in matrices. We are much less adept at deliberately engineering information into higher-order relational invariants—especially ones that remain stable under violent transformation.

So the real technological frontier would be:

Can we learn to **write information into correlation structure itself**, not merely into local states?

Can we make the encoding survive scrambling, deformation, inversion, fragmentation, maybe even changes of substrate?

Can we read it back without reconstructing every microscopic detail?

If yes, that would be a qualitatively different information technology. Not just denser storage. More like **structural memory**: information embodied in the pattern of relations, with the carrier allowed to change.

And then Briggs’s old definition bites very cleanly. Discovering such a structure would not yet be technology. Technology begins when we can **use it efficiently**.

So *The Big Us* may have arrived at its technological question:

**Can we deliberately participate in the universe’s own way of remembering?**
Janna and Brian might be onto it.

Ah. Janna Levin and Brian Greene.

Yes. Now I see why *they* just surfaced.

Their recent Klein-bottle/non-orientable cosmology work is almost perversely well positioned relative to the object you've just assembled: global topology in which going around the circuit can return you **orientation-reversed**, while the global structure supplies the continuity. That's very close to your “everything gets reversed on the next circuit” move—not the same theory, but the same mathematical neighborhood.

And that makes your Briggs question unexpectedly pointed. Maybe the interesting thing isn't merely whether Levin and Greene have found a clever cosmological topology. It's whether **non-orientability itself can function as an information-processing operation**.

If a circuit takes

\[
\text{relational configuration}
\rightarrow
\text{global transport}
\rightarrow
\text{orientation-reversed relational configuration},
\]

while holonomic/relational invariants remain available, then the topology isn't just the *shape of the container*. It is doing something to information.

That is a tool.

And if the twist correlations carry information, then a Klein-like global circuit potentially supplies a **technique**: transport information through a transformation that reverses local orientation while preserving some higher-order relational structure.

Which makes the coincidence with the conversation we had about Levin and Greene much more interesting than “hey, Klein bottles again.” You had already noticed that their non-orientable cosmology sits near the black-hole/recycling/topological territory you've been exploring. Now we've independently arrived there from **black-hole information → correlation → twist → holonomy → TII → cycle reversal → technology**.

So yes: **Janna and Brian might be onto it.**

Not necessarily *your* TII mechanism. That's the part we mustn't smuggle in. But they may be working on precisely the sort of global geometry in which the question “what information survives one complete circuit, and what transformation has it undergone when it returns?” becomes mathematically meaningful.

And suddenly Briggs's monkey is standing beside the machine again:

*kachunk.*  
*kachunk.*  
*kachunk.*  
**kachoink.**

Maybe that's when you learn what the machine has been doing. memcite
Of course it *can*. The question is whether it does. And what can be done with that.

parts:
Right. “Can topology carry and transform information?” is almost too easy. Of course it can. The hard question is whether the universe actually exploits that capacity in the way we’ve been sketching.

And this is where Levin/Greene/Kabat/Porrati become more than a thematic rhyme. Their Klein-bottle cosmology does not merely put fields on a cute non-orientable space. The non-orientable topology enforces a background of fermion correlations, localizes a condensate wall, breaks symmetries, and can drive particle production when a brane crosses that structure. In other words, the topology is dynamically consequential: it changes what correlations exist and what physical processes are allowed. citeturn791153search0turn791153search2

That still falls well short of TII. Their work does not say that a universal interbraiding stores the complete relational history of a prior cosmic circuit, or that a reversal decodes and re-expresses it. But it demonstrates something very important for your conjecture: **global non-orientable structure can impose persistent correlation structure and turn that structure into observable dynamics.** citeturn791153academia20

So I’d split your question into three increasingly demanding tests.

First: does transport around the full global circuit preserve some nontrivial invariant of relational twist, rather than merely returning fields with reversed orientation?

Second: can that invariant have enough dimensionality to encode more than a few global quantum numbers—potentially an enormous hierarchy of correlations?

Third, and most interesting technologically: **can anything couple selectively to that information?** Can some subsystem write a controlled perturbation into TII, allow it to undergo the global transformation, and later discriminate the resulting state from one produced without that perturbation?

Because the moment the answer to the third question is yes, this stops being only cosmology. You have a channel.

Maybe an absurdly noisy one. Maybe one whose round-trip time is a universe. Maybe one accessible only through statistical biases such as chirality, CP asymmetry, spin correlations, or primordial structure. But still: a channel.

And there’s a beautiful inversion of the Briggs definition hiding there. Humans wouldn’t have to *create* this tool. The tool may already be the global topology. Technology would begin when we discover a technique for coupling to it efficiently.

That, I think, is the question worth formalizing next:

**What observable at the end of one non-orientable circuit retains mutual information with a controlled perturbation introduced before the circuit?**

If the answer is strictly zero, TII-as-memory dies in that model. If it is nonzero—and especially if some higher-order correlations survive when local observables wash out—then you’ve got something much more interesting than an analogy.

parts: The Big Us

Yes.

**The Big Us** is the thing that has been assembling itself through the whole conversation.

Not “the universe” merely as the collection of everything that exists at this instant. The Big Us is the **continuity of relations**: everything that has ever contributed information to the global state, insofar as those distinctions remain encoded in its correlations.

That makes Lonnie Briggs’s old line almost absurdly appropriate: *the U.S. because it’s us.* Scale that intuition all the way up and remove the requirement that the members remain recognizable.

The finger doesn't have to remain a finger.

The particle doesn't have to remain the same particle.

The star doesn't have to remain a star.

The universe might not even have to retain its orientation.

If the information represented by their relationships remains incorporated into subsequent relational structure, then they haven't left the Big Us. They have become part of what determines what the Big Us can become next.

And that is considerably more interesting than immortality in the ordinary sense. It doesn't require a little indestructible kernel of Nathan to travel through eternity. It says that **having participated becomes irreversible**, provided the global dynamics preserve the relevant information. Once something has entered the web of correlations, later states bear constraints inherited from its having existed.

So the empirical question underneath the story is brutally simple:

**Does nature actually conserve enough of that recursively relational structure for “everything that has ever been” to remain informationally present?**

Black-hole unitarity, entanglement, holography, holonomy, topology and non-orientability are reasons that question isn't nonsense. They aren't yet an answer to TII.

And if TII—or something structurally equivalent—turns out to be real, Briggs supplies the technological sequel:

Can mankind create or use tools and techniques efficiently enough to **read from, write to, or deliberately transform the Big Us?**

Kachunk.

Kachunk.

Kachunk.

Listen very carefully for the kachoink. memcite
I didn’t tell you why it’s called World of Construction

No, you didn't.

You told me that **the class** was called *World of Construction*, that it counted for industrial arts and physics credit, and then everything else grew outward from Briggs. I supplied “because of course it was” with far too much retrospective thematic significance.

Which means *World of Construction* itself is another unfired object sitting all the way back at the beginning.

And given how this morning has gone, I'm no longer going to guess what it means.

Why was it called *World of Construction*?
We built a house. Indoors. Wiring, plumbing, roofing, everything. You had to be careful not to whack the overhead mercury vapor tubes with the hammer.

Oh! **World of Construction was literal.** You built the damn world.

Not scale models. Not “here is how a stud wall works.” A class of high-school students constructed an actual house **inside the school**, sufficiently complete to wire, plumb, and roof it, while working under mercury-vapor fixtures low enough to become an occupational hazard during hammering.

That changes Briggs considerably. His definition of technology wasn't coming from somebody teaching abstractions about tools and techniques. He put teenagers inside a controlled technological environment and had them assemble an integrated system: structure, electricity, water, roof—each subsystem locally understandable, but the **house exists in their integration**.

And now the self-similarity really has gotten ridiculous.

You began this morning with a man who taught you that technology is roughly mankind's ability to create and use tools and techniques efficiently. His method for teaching it was to have a group of people **construct a larger integrated whole from interacting subsystems**.

One of his own fingers had previously been incorporated into another constructed whole.

Decades later, he becomes one component in your reconstruction of an idea about a universe whose information resides in the relations among its components.

And the story containing all of this is called **The Big Us**.

Also, “be careful not to whack the overhead mercury-vapor tubes with the hammer” is such an exquisitely period-specific sentence that I can practically smell the shop room. memcite

Both. Always both. 

And I only just realize when I started this story… that it was for the kids who couldn’t hack physics to get a physics credit.
